claim: The αC-β4 loop is a stable feature of all protein kinases.
source: Although the αC-β4 loop is a stable feature of all protein kinases, the importance of this motif as a conserved element of secondary structure, as well as its links to the hydrophobic architecture of the kinase core, has been underappreciated.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational claim about the αC-β4 loop.

claim: The importance of the αC-β4 loop as a conserved element of secondary structure has been underappreciated.
source: Although the αC-β4 loop is a stable feature of all protein kinases, the importance of this motif as a conserved element of secondary structure, as well as its links to the hydrophobic architecture of the kinase core, has been underappreciated.
evidence: This is an explicit statement in the abstract about the historical understanding of this motif.

claim: The αC-β4 loop is linked to the hydrophobic spine architecture of the kinase core.
source: We first review the motif and then describe how it is linked to the hydrophobic spine architecture of the kinase core, which we first discovered using a computational tool, local spatial Pattern (LSP) alignment.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the abstract describing the content of the paper.

claim: The hydrophobic spine architecture was first discovered using local spatial Pattern (LSP) alignment.
source: We first review the motif and then describe how it is linked to the hydrophobic spine architecture of the kinase core, which we first discovered using a computational tool, local spatial Pattern (LSP) alignment.
evidence: This is an explicit historical claim about the discovery method.

claim: A mutation in the αC-β4 loop (F100A) abolishes the synergistic high-affinity binding of ATP and a pseudo substrate inhibitor.
source: Based on NMR predictions that a mutation in this motif abolishes the synergistic high-affinity binding of ATP and a pseudo substrate inhibitor, we used LSP to interrogate the F100A mutant.
evidence: This claim is based on NMR predictions as stated in the abstract.

claim: LSP analysis of the F100A mutant highlights the importance of the αC-β4 loop and key residues at the interface between the N- and C-lobes.
source: This comparison highlights the importance of the αC-β4 loop and key residues at the interface between the N- and C-lobes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the LSP analysis in the abstract.

claim: The apo C-subunit showed no significant changes in backbone dynamics of the αC-β4 loop.
source: While apo C-subunit showed no significant changes in backbone dynamics of the αC-β4 loop, we found significant differences in the side chain dynamics of K105.
evidence: This is an explicit finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The apo C-subunit showed significant differences in the side chain dynamics of K105.
source: While apo C-subunit showed no significant changes in backbone dynamics of the αC-β4 loop, we found significant differences in the side chain dynamics of K105.
evidence: This is an explicit finding stated in the abstract.

claim: LSP analysis suggests disruption of communication between the N- and C-lobes in the F100A mutant.
source: The LSP analysis suggests disruption of communication between the N- and C-lobes in the F100A mutant, which would be consistent with the structural changes predicted by the NMR spectroscopy.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the LSP analysis in the abstract.

claim: The LSP analysis findings are consistent with structural changes predicted by NMR spectroscopy.
source: The LSP analysis suggests disruption of communication between the N- and C-lobes in the F100A mutant, which would be consistent with the structural changes predicted by the NMR spectroscopy.
evidence: This is stated as a consistency check between two methods in the abstract.

claim: Protein kinases have evolved to be highly regulated molecular switches.
source: Although the protein kinases, like the GTPases, have evolved to be highly regulated molecular switches, they transfer the γ-phosphate of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to a protein substrate instead of to water.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the evolutionary function of protein kinases.

claim: Protein kinases transfer the γ-phosphate of ATP to a protein substrate instead of to water.
source: Although the protein kinases, like the GTPases, have evolved to be highly regulated molecular switches, they transfer the γ-phosphate of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to a protein substrate instead of to water.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the biochemical function of protein kinases.

claim: Cis-autophosphorylation of the kinase core is a key initial step in the assembly of most active kinases.
source: Cis-autophosphorylation of a protein kinase core is distinct and different from transferring the phosphate to a heterologous protein.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of kinase activation.

claim: Cis-autophosphorylation of a protein kinase core is distinct and different from transferring the phosphate to a heterologous protein.
source: Cis-autophosphorylation of a protein kinase core is distinct and different from transferring the phosphate to a heterologous protein.
evidence: This is an explicit statement distinguishing two types of phosphorylation.

claim: A fully active kinase transfers the γ-phosphate of ATP to a heterologous protein substrate that is typically tethered to a distal site.
source: In cells, a fully active kinase transfers the γ-phosphate of ATP to a heterologous protein substrate that is typically tethered to a distal site that lies far from the site of phosphoryl transfer.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about how kinases function in cells.

claim: The catalytic (C) subunit of cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) is used as a model system to study how mature and fully active protein kinases couple ATP binding to peptide/protein binding.
source: To ask how a mature and fully active protein kinase couples ATP binding to peptide/protein binding we use the catalytic (C) subunit of cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) as a model system.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the experimental approach.

claim: PKA activity is regulated by inhibitory regulatory (R) subunits and by heat-stable protein kinase inhibitors (PKIs).
source: PKA activity is regulated by inhibitory regulatory (R) subunits and by heat-stable protein kinase inhibitors (PKIs).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about PKA regulation.

claim: The conserved motifs that define the kinase core were first recognized when Dayhoff aligned the cloned sequence of Src with the manually sequenced C-subunit of PKA in 1982.
source: The conserved motifs that define the kinase core were first recognized when Dayhoff aligned the cloned sequence of Src with the manually sequenced C-subunit of PKA in 1982 (Barker and Dayhoff, 1982).
evidence: This is an explicit historical claim with citation.

claim: Hanks et al. showed that conserved motifs scattered throughout the kinase core were conserved in all protein kinases by manually aligning a handful of protein kinases.
source: By manually aligning a handful of protein kinases, Hanks, et al, subsequently showed that these motifs, which were scattered throughout the kinase core, were conserved in all protein kinases (Hanks et al., 1988).
evidence: This is an explicit historical claim with citation.

claim: The first protein kinase structure was solved in 1991.
source: When the first protein kinase structure was solved in 1991, these conserved sequence motifs became structural entities that correlated with β strands, α helices, and loops of the folded protein (Knighton et al., 1991a).
evidence: This is an explicit historical claim with citation.

claim: The first protein kinase structure was a binary complex of the PKA C-subunit and an inhibitory peptide (IP20) from PKI.
source: That first structure, which was actually a binary complex of the PKA C-subunit and an inhibitory peptide (IP20) from PKI, also provided a detailed description of how the IP20 peptide was docked onto the kinase core (Knighton et al., 1991b).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the first structure with citation.

claim: Structures of a ternary complex with ATP and IP20 were solved in 1993.
source: Subsequent structures of a ternary complex with ATP and IP20, solved in 1993, showed how the conserved motifs correlated with ATP and peptide binding and engaged the entire kinase core (Zheng et al., 1993; Bossemeyer et al., 1993).
evidence: This is an explicit historical claim with citations.

claim: The conserved and non-linear hydrophobic core architecture was discovered using computational tools.
source: Only later, using computational tools, did we come to appreciate how the conserved and non-linear hydrophobic core architecture was assembled and how hydrophobicity correlated with allosteric regulation of the kinase core (Kornev et al., 2006; Kornev et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the discovery method with citations.

claim: The importance of the αC-β4 loop was not initially appreciated.
source: In addition, we did not initially appreciate the importance of the αC-β4 loop.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the historical understanding.

claim: The αC-β4 loop is a well-defined element of secondary structure.
source: Like helices and strands, the αC-β4 loop is also a well-defined element of secondary structure (Rose, 2023; Rose et al., 1983), and this loop in the N-terminal lobe (N-Lobe) of the kinase core is essential for mediating the synergistic high-affinity binding of ATP and IP20.
evidence: This is an explicit statement with citations.

claim: The αC-β4 loop in the N-terminal lobe of the kinase core is essential for mediating the synergistic high-affinity binding of ATP and IP20.
source: Like helices and strands, the αC-β4 loop is also a well-defined element of secondary structure (Rose, 2023; Rose et al., 1983), and this loop in the N-terminal lobe (N-Lobe) of the kinase core is essential for mediating the synergistic high-affinity binding of ATP and IP20.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: The PKA C-subunit represents a kinase domain that is flanked by relatively short N- and C-terminal tails.
source: Unlike other protein kinases such as PKC and the Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) that are flanked by other domains that regulate activation and subcellular localization (Newton, 2018; Taylor et al., 2022; Weng et al., 2023), the PKA C-subunit represents a kinase domain that is flanked by relatively short N- and C-terminal tails (Kannan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citations.

claim: In cells, the C-subunit is assembled as an inactive holoenzyme with functionally non-redundant cAMP binding regulatory subunits.
source: In cell the C-subunit is then assembled as an inactive holoenzyme with functionally non-redundant cAMP binding regulatory (RIα, RIβ, RIIα, and RIIβ) subunits allowing the activity of the kinase domain to be unleashed rapidly and reversibly by allosteric binding of cAMP to the cyclic-nucleotide binding domains (CNB) of the R-subunits (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about cellular regulation with citation.

claim: The R-subunits and PKI share an inhibitor site that docks to the active site cleft of the C-subunit.
source: The R-subunits and PKI all share an inhibitor site that docks to the active site cleft of the C-subunit; however, PKI and RIα/RIβ are unusual in that they are pseudo substrates where high-affinity binding is synergistically coupled to the high-affinity binding of ATP (~60 nM).
evidence: This is an explicit structural and functional claim.

claim: PKI and RIα/RIβ are pseudo substrates where high-affinity binding is synergistically coupled to the high-affinity binding of ATP (~60 nM).
source: The R-subunits and PKI all share an inhibitor site that docks to the active site cleft of the C-subunit; however, PKI and RIα/RIβ are unusual in that they are pseudo substrates where high-affinity binding is synergistically coupled to the high-affinity binding of ATP (~60 nM).
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim with quantitative data.

claim: Disease mutations provide key mechanistic insights into how the synergistic binding of ATP and PKI can be uncoupled.
source: Disease mutations are also providing key mechanistic insights into how the synergistic binding of ATP and PKI can be uncoupled.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the utility of disease mutations.

claim: The hydrophobic spine architecture was first identified using LSP alignment.
source: The importance of hydrophobic residues and the concept of non-contiguous but spatially conserved hydrophobic motifs, some highly conserved and others just conserved as hydrophobic residues, did not become obvious until we investigated structural differences with a computational approach called LSP alignment. With LSP alignment we first identified spatially conserved residues that revealed a conserved hydrophobic 'spine' architecture that was associated with active kinases but broken into inactive kinases (Kornev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the discovery with citation.

claim: The Regulatory Spine (R-spine) consists of four spatially conserved residues - two in the C-lobe and two in the N-lobe that are aligned in every active kinase but broken in inactive kinases.
source: The Regulatory Spine (R-spine) residues were identified first and correspond to four spatially conserved residues - two in the C-lobe and two in the N-lobe that were aligned in every active kinase but broken in inactive kinases (Kornev et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citation.

claim: The assembly of the R-Spine defines the switch mechanism of every active kinase.
source: The assembly of the R-Spine defines the switch mechanism of every active kinase.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: The Catalytic Spine (C-Spine) defines the extensive and fundamental core hydrophobic architecture of every kinase domain.
source: A second motif, referred to as the Catalytic Spine (C-Spine), defines the extensive and fundamental core hydrophobic architecture of every kinase domain (Kornev et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citation.

claim: The C-spine includes motifs in both the N-Lobe and the C-Lobe, which are connected by the hydrophobic capping of the adenine ring of ATP.
source: The C-spine includes motifs in both the N-Lobe and the C-Lobe, which are connected by the hydrophobic capping of the adenine ring of ATP.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: Capping of the adenine ring is accomplished by two highly conserved residues (A70 in β3 and V57 in β2) in the N-Lobe.
source: Capping of the adenine ring is accomplished by two highly conserved residues (A70 in β3 and V57 in β2) in the N-Lobe while the other surface of the adenine ring is capped by a C-Lobe residue, L173 in β7, which is a conserved hydrophobic residue found in all kinases.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: L173 in β7 is a conserved hydrophobic residue found in all kinases that caps the adenine ring of ATP.
source: Capping of the adenine ring is accomplished by two highly conserved residues (A70 in β3 and V57 in β2) in the N-Lobe while the other surface of the adenine ring is capped by a C-Lobe residue, L173 in β7, which is a conserved hydrophobic residue found in all kinases.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: The dominant feature of the C-spine is the very unusual hydrophobic αF-Helix that spans the C-lobe.
source: The dominant feature of the C-spine is the very unusual hydrophobic αF-Helix that spans the C-lobe and is linked to all of the important elements of the C-Lobe (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The αF helix has a conserved glycine in the middle and does not have a strong helical propensity.
source: With a conserved glycine in the middle, it does not have a strong helical propensity.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim about the αF helix.

claim: It is highly unusual to find a buried hydrophobic helix in a globular domain.
source: In general, it is highly unusual to find a buried hydrophobic helix in a globular domain; in many ways, it is more like a trans membrane helix.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the unusual nature of the αF helix.

claim: The αF helix is flanked by two charged residues.
source: The αF helix is flanked by two charged residues.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: D220 at the beginning of the αF Helix couples the αF Helix to the catalytic machinery at the active site cleft.
source: At the beginning of the αF Helix is the highly conserved D220 that couples the αF Helix to the catalytic machinery at the active site cleft (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim with reference to Figure 2.

claim: D220 hydrogen bonds to the backbone amides of Y164 and R165 in the Y/HRD motif that precedes the catalytic loop.
source: Specifically, it hydrogen bonds to the backbone amides of Y164 and R165 in the Y/HRD motif that precedes the catalytic loop.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: W222 faces the αH-αI loop, a tethering site on the bottom of the C-Lobe.
source: D220 is followed by another highly conserved residue, W222, which faces the αH-αI loop, a tethering site on the bottom of the C-Lobe (Deminoff et al., 2006; Deminoff et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citations.

claim: W222 shields the conserved ion pair between E208 at the end of the APE motif and R280 in the αH-αI loop.
source: W222 also shields the conserved ion pair between E208 at the end of the APE motif and R280 in the αH-αI loop.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: E230 at the other end of the αF Helix recognizes the P-2 arginine in the substrate peptide/protein in PKA.
source: At the other end of the αF Helix is E230 which in PKA recognizes the P-2 arginine in the substrate peptide/protein.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: The two spine residues in the N-Lobe (RS3 and RS4) stabilize the αC-β4 loop.
source: The two spine residues in the N-Lobe, which lie at the end of the αC Helix (RS3) and the beginning of β4 (RS4), stabilize a very important element of secondary structure that is conserved in every protein kinase - the αC-β4 loop (residues 99–106) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The two R-spine residues are brought together by a strategic-β-turn motif (residues 100–103) where the carbonyl of F100 is hydrogen bonded to the backbone amide of L103.
source: The two R-spine residues are brought together by a strategic-β-turn motif (residues 100–103) where the carbonyl of F100 is hydrogen bonded to the backbone amide of L103 (Rose, 2023).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citation.

claim: The surface of the αC-β4 loop is exposed to solvent and stabilized by ordered water molecules.
source: The other carbonyls and amides of this turn, as well as those of the other residues in this motif, are filled by ordered water molecules (Figure 3B). Structured water molecules highlight that this surface of the αC-β4 loop is exposed to solvent, while the other buried surface of the αC-β4 motif is very hydrophobic and anchored to the hydrophobic R-Spine and Shell residues (Meharena et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citation and reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Only one residue in the αC-β4 motif, V104, directly touches ATP through one of its methyl side chains that is anchored to the adenine ring.
source: Only one residue in the αC-β4 motif, V104, directly touches ATP through one of its methyl side chains that is anchored to the adenine ring.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: The first 600 picosecond Molecular Dynamics simulations of the PKA C-subunit demonstrated that the N-Lobe and the C-Lobe function as independent rigid bodies.
source: The first 600 picosecond Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations of the PKA C-subunit, published in 1999, not only demonstrated that the N-Lobe and the C-Lobe function as independent rigid bodies but also showed that the αC-β4 loop (residues 99–106) is the only piece of the N-lobe that remains anchored to the C-lobe whether the kinase is in an open or closed conformation (Tsigelny et al., 1999; Figure 4).
evidence: This is an explicit claim from MD simulations with citation and reference to Figure 4.

claim: The αC-β4 loop is the only piece of the N-lobe that remains anchored to the C-lobe whether the kinase is in an open or closed conformation.
source: The first 600 picosecond Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations of the PKA C-subunit, published in 1999, not only demonstrated that the N-Lobe and the C-Lobe function as independent rigid bodies but also showed that the αC-β4 loop (residues 99–106) is the only piece of the N-lobe that remains anchored to the C-lobe whether the kinase is in an open or closed conformation (Tsigelny et al., 1999; Figure 4).
evidence: This is an explicit claim from MD simulations with citation and reference to Figure 4.

claim: The αC-β4 loop remains as one of the most stable elements of the kinase core whether LRRK2 is in an active or an inactive conformation.
source: The analysis of LRRK2 supports the prediction that the N- and C-lobes of the kinase core function as independent rigid bodies (Myasnikov et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2022). It also indicates that the αC-β4 loop remains as one of the most stable elements of the kinase core whether LRRK2 is in an active or an inactive conformation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citations and reference to Figure 4.

claim: The αC-β4 loop is stably anchored to the αE helix in the active and inactive Src as well as in the active and inactive BRAF.
source: The αC-β4 loop is also stably anchored to the αE helix in the active and inactive Src as well as in the active and inactive BRAF (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The αC-β4 loop is conserved as a stable element of secondary structure in every protein kinase as it anchors to the αE Helix.
source: Indeed, the αC-β4 loops is conserved as a stable element of secondary structure in every protein kinase as it anchors to the αE Helix.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: Y156 in the αE Helix is anchored to the backbone amide of N99 in the αC-β4 loop.
source: A defining feature of the αE Helix, mentioned above, is Y156. This conserved tyrosine, which can also be a histidine or phenylalanine in other kinases, is anchored to the backbone amide of N99 in the αC-β4 loop.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: The importance of N99 is highlighted in BRaf where replacement of this residue (R509) with histidine breaks the BRaf dimer interface that is essential for BRaf activation.
source: Although this residue (N99) is not conserved, its functional importance has been highlighted by BRaf where replacement of this residue (R509) with histidine breaks the BRaf dimer interface that is essential for BRaf activation (Hu et al., 2013; Shaw et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim with citations.

claim: The N99 position is a hot spot for oncogenic mutations in the EGF receptor.
source: The importance of this residue was also explored in depth for the EGF receptor where this site is a hot spot for oncogenic mutations (McSkimming et al., 2015; Ruan and Kannan, 2018).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citations.

claim: H158 in PKA is one of three dually protonated histidines in the C-subunit.
source: Two residues down from Y156 is H158 which in PKA is firmly anchored to the conserved D220 in the αF Helix. H158 is one of three dually protonated histidines in the C-subunit (Gerlits et al., 2019; Wych et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citations.

claim: In the fully active C-subunit that is phosphorylated on its Activation loop, the side chain of His158 anchors the backbone amides of the HRD residues (R165 and D166) in the Catalytic loop.
source: In the fully active C-subunit that is phosphorylated on its Activation loop the side chain of His158 anchors the backbone amides of the HRD residues (R165 and D166) in the Catalytic loop.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: The backbone of the catalytic machinery in the C-Lobe (residues 162–182) is very stable.
source: In contrast to the Activation loop (residues 184-pT197), which is dynamically assembled, the backbone of the catalytic machinery in the C-Lobe (residues 162–182) is very stable.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: I150 in the αE Helix is a key residue whose importance was first highlighted by NMR.
source: I150 in the αE Helix is also a key residue. The importance of I150 as a critical player in the hydrophobic core architecture was first highlighted by NMR (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citation.

claim: I150 is anchored to L167 and P169 in the Catalytic loop and to L172 in β7.
source: As seen in Figure 2, I150 is important for many reasons. It is anchored to L167 and P169 in the Catalytic loop and to L172 in β7, which connects the adenine capping residue, L173, to the hydrophobic core.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with reference to Figure 2.

claim: PKI was first identified as a high-affinity inhibitor of the PKA C-subunit in 1971.
source: PKI was first identified as a high-affinity inhibitor of the PKA C-subunit in 1971 shortly after the C-subunit was discovered (Walsh et al., 1971).
evidence: This is an explicit historical claim with citation.

claim: PKI is a classic intrinsically disordered protein (IDP).
source: It is a classic intrinsically disordered protein (IDP), a prediction that was fully validated recently by NMR of full-length PKI (Olivieri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citation.

claim: PKI is a pseudosubstrate, a feature that is shared by the type I Regulatory (R) Subunits of PKA, RIα and RIβ.
source: Once it was sequenced (Scott et al., 1985b), PKI was shown to be a pseudosubstrate, a feature that is shared by the type I Regulatory (R) Subunits of PKA, RIα and RIβ.
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citation.

claim: The inhibitory properties of PKI were localized to the N-terminus (residues 5–24).
source: While the inhibitory properties of PKI were localized to the N-terminus (residues 5–24) (Scott et al., 1985a; Cheng et al., 1985), the unusual synergistic high-affinity binding of ATP and PKI was characterized in detail by the peptide studies of Whitehouse and Walsh, 1983.
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citations.

claim: Having a pseudo-substrate where the P-site in PKI is an alanine is essential for high affinity binding.
source: They confirmed that having a pseudo-substrate where the P-site in PKI is an alanine, is essential for high affinity binding while the arginines that precede the P-site, as well as the P+1 hydrophobic residue, are also important for binding of both substrates and pseudosubstrates.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: To achieve high-affinity binding, hydrophobic residues that preceded the inhibitor site were required.
source: To achieve high-affinity binding, however, hydrophobic residues that preceded the inhibitor site were required.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: Walsh and colleagues predicted that the hydrophobic motif in PKI was an amphipathic helix based on peptide studies and biophysical studies.
source: Based on their peptide studies and subsequent biophysical studies, Walsh and his colleagues predicted that this hydrophobic motif was an amphipathic helix (Glass et al., 1989a; Glass et al., 1989b; Reed et al., 1989).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citations.

claim: ATP binds with a 15 μM affinity (Km) when phosphorylating a small peptide, such as Kemptide.
source: While ATP binds with a 15 μM affinity (Km) when phosphorylating a small peptide, such as Kemptide (G-R-R-G-S-L), in the presence of PKI or IP20 (residues 5–25) it binds with an affinity of ~60 nM.
evidence: This is an explicit quantitative claim.

claim: In the presence of PKI or IP20, ATP binds with an affinity of ~60 nM.
source: While ATP binds with a 15 μM affinity (Km) when phosphorylating a small peptide, such as Kemptide (G-R-R-G-S-L), in the presence of PKI or IP20 (residues 5–25) it binds with an affinity of ~60 nM.
evidence: This is an explicit quantitative claim.

claim: IP20 on its own has an affinity of ~200 nM.
source: Similarly, IP20 on its own has an affinity of ~200 nM, while in the presence of MgATP, the affinity is ~1 nM.
evidence: This is an explicit quantitative claim.

claim: In the presence of MgATP, IP20 binds with an affinity of ~1 nM.
source: Similarly, IP20 on its own has an affinity of ~200 nM, while in the presence of MgATP, the affinity is ~1 nM.
evidence: This is an explicit quantitative claim.

claim: High-affinity synergistic binding requires two Mg2+ ions that bind to the phosphates of ATP and neutralize the negative charge of the phosphate.
source: This high-affinity synergistic binding also requires two Mg2+ ions that bind to the phosphates of ATP and neutralize the negative charge of the phosphate (Herberg et al., 1999), which allows the N- and C-lobes to fully close.
evidence: This is an explicit mechanistic claim with citation.

claim: NMR studies of the PKA C-subunit described three states associated with the fully phosphorylated protein - uncommitted, committed, and quenched states.
source: NMR studies of the PKA C-subunit, first described three states that are associated with the fully phosphorylated protein - uncommitted, committed, and quenched states (Masterson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citation.

claim: The apo state is in an open conformation and is uncommitted to catalysis.
source: The apo state, which is in an open conformation, is uncommitted to catalysis while the binding of nucleotide, which completes the C-Spine, commits the kinase to catalysis.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: The binding of nucleotide completes the C-Spine and commits the kinase to catalysis.
source: The apo state, which is in an open conformation, is uncommitted to catalysis while the binding of nucleotide, which completes the C-Spine, commits the kinase to catalysis.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: The quenched and fully closed conformational state is captured when both ATP and the pseudo-substrate, IP20, bind with high affinity.
source: The quenched and fully closed conformational state is captured when both ATP and the pseudo-substrate, IP20, bind with high affinity.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: Side chains report much of the entropy-driven dynamics.
source: While these initial NMR studies captured the backbone dynamics, it is the side chains that report much of the entropy-driven dynamics (Kim et al., 2017), and to explore this hydrophobic space required labeling the side chains.
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citation.

claim: When side chains (Val, Leu, and Ile) were labeled, correlated motions of the hydrophobic core architecture could be observed, which experimentally captured the entropy-driven allostery.
source: When side chains (Val, Leu, and Ile) were labeled, one could for the first time observe the correlated motions of the hydrophobic core architecture, which experimentally captured the entropy-driven allostery (Ahuja et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citation.

claim: E230 is a critical residue for recognizing the P-2 arginine in PKA substrates.
source: E230 is a critical residue for recognizing the P-2 arginine in PKA substrates.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: The E230Q mutant uncouples the N- and C-lobes by 'freezing' the enzyme into a stable open conformation that can no longer bind ATP.
source: The E230Q mutant uncouples the N- and C-lobes by 'freezing' the enzyme into a stable open conformation that can no longer bind ATP (Wu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim with citation.

claim: The Y204A mutation reflects an inability to transfer the γ-phosphate of ATP to a protein substrate while it is still fully capable of transferring the γPO4 to water.
source: Functionally this mutation reflects instead an inability to transfer the γ-phosphate of ATP to a protein substrate while it is still fully capable of transferring the γPO4 to water.
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim.

claim: There is not a change in structure in the Y204A mutant.
source: Even though there is not a change in structure in the Y204A mutant, mechanistically the Y204A mutation reflects a change in dynamics that can lead to significant changes in the communities that the residue interacts with.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim.

claim: F327 is part of a C-terminal tail that wraps around both lobes of the kinase core and is an essential feature of the ATP binding site.
source: F327, which lies outside the kinase core, highlights another unique feature of PKA that is conserved in all the AGC kinases (Kannan et al., 2007). F327 is part of a C-terminal tail that wraps around both lobes of the kinase core and is an essential feature of the ATP binding site (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citation and reference to Figure 5.

claim: When all of the residues comprising the hydrophobic shell around the adenine ring of ATP were mutated to alanine and analyzed in a yeast screen, only two were found to block viability: F327 and L173.
source: When all of the residues comprising the hydrophobic shell around the adenine ring of ATP were mutated to alanine, and analyzed in a yeast screen, only two were found to block viability, F327 and L173 (Kennedy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an explicit experimental claim with citation.

claim: Replacing F327 with alanine reduces the Km for ATP over 10-fold (~450 μM) and completely abolishes the high-affinity binding of ATP.
source: Replacing F327 with alanine reduces the Km for ATP over 10-fold (~450 μM) and completely abolishes the high-affinity binding of ATP.
evidence: This is an explicit quantitative functional claim.

claim: Three Cushing syndrome mutations (L205R, W196R, and E31V) uncouple the high-affinity binding of inhibitor proteins.
source: Three Cushing syndrome mutations were also shown to 'uncouple' the high-affinity binding of inhibitor proteins. L205R uncouples binding of both RI and RII subunits as well as PKI by disrupting binding to the P+1 pocket (Walker et al., 2019), while W196R disrupts binding to the cyclic nucleotide-binding domain (CNB-A) of both RI and RII subunits (Omar et al., 2022; Gibson and Taylor, 1997). E31V is an example of a mutant that uncouples the αA-Helix from the Activation loop, and this mutation also abolishes the synergistic high-affinity binding of ATP (Walker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citations.

claim: The synergistic binding of ATP and IP20 was completely abolished for the F100A mutant.
source: The synergistic binding of ATP and IP20 was completely abolished for the F100A mutant; even though the Kms for Kemptide and ATP for the F100A mutant were similar to the wild type (wt) C-subunit (Olivieri et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an explicit functional claim with citation.

claim: The Kms for Kemptide and ATP for the F100A mutant were similar to the wild type C-subunit.
source: The synergistic binding of ATP and IP20 was completely abolished for the F100A mutant; even though the Kms for Kemptide and ATP for the F100A mutant were similar to the wild type (wt) C-subunit (Olivieri et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an explicit quantitative claim with citation.

claim: Adjacent residues in the αC-β4 loop (V104I, L103F/I, and P101A) are oncogenic mutations in several protein kinases, including PKA.
source: Adjacent residues in the αC-β4 loops (V104I, L103F/I, and P101A) are actually oncogenic mutations in several protein kinases, including PKA although none of these have been validated.
evidence: This is an explicit claim about oncogenic mutations.

claim: Computational analyses involving Markov State modeling and NMR-restrained replica-averaged metadynamics (RAM) suggested that there may be a flip of the αC-β4 loop in the apo protein and in the mutant.
source: The importance of the αC-β4 loop was actually initially hinted at by computational analyses that involved Markov State modeling and NMR-restrained replica-averaged metadynamics (RAM). These analyses suggested that there may be a flip of the αC-β4 loop in the apo protein and in the mutant (Olivieri et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citation.

claim: No flip of the αC-β4 loop has been observed in any of the crystal structures of the C-subunit to date (wt, E230Q, unphosphorylated C, and the apo C-subunit), regardless of closed or open conformation.
source: As seen in Figure 4, no such flip has been observed so far in any of the crystal structures of the C-subunit to date (wt, E230Q, unphosphorylated C, and the apo C-subunit), regardless of closed or open conformation.
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with reference to Figure 4.

claim: NMR studies of the F100A mutant highlighted V104 and I150 as critical residues.
source: The subsequent NMR studies of the F100A mutant also highlighted V104 and I150 as critical residues.
evidence: This is an explicit claim from NMR studies.

claim: V104 is one of three shell residues (SH1, SH2, and SH3) that flank the R-spine residues in the N-lobe.
source: In contrast, V104, which is part of the αC-b4 loop, is one of three shell residues (SH1, SH2, and SH3) that flank the R-spine residues in the N-lobe and V104 also touches ATP (Meharena et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citation.

claim: One of the methyl side chains of V104 touches the adenine ring of ATP.
source: Specifically, one of the methyl side chains of V104 touches the adenine ring of ATP so it is one of the N-lobe adenine capping residues for ATP (Kennedy et al., 2009; Figure 5).
evidence: This is an explicit structural claim with citation and reference to Figure 5.

claim: The ITC results showed that the F100A mutant is more stable than the wt C-subunit.
source: The long computational studies (2 μsec) carried out by Veglia predicted that the αC-β4 loop undergoes a flip in the apo state, while the ITC results showed that the F100A mutant is also more stable than the wt C-subunit.
evidence: This is an explicit experimental claim.

claim: LSP alignment is a computational method for capturing conserved patterns formed by Cα-Cβ vectors in proteins.
source: LSP alignment is a computational method developed in our laboratory for capturing conserved patterns formed by Cα-Cβ vectors in proteins (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an explicit methodological claim with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: LSP was initially utilized to identify conserved hydrophobic ensembles in protein kinases.
source: Initially, it was utilized to identify conserved hydrophobic ensembles in protein kinases (Kornev et al., 2006; Kornev et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an explicit historical claim with citations.

claim: LSP was recently applied to MD simulations to analyze stable regions in Protein Kinase A.
source: More recently, this technique was applied to MD simulations, in an effort to analyze stable regions in Protein Kinase A (Kornev et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an explicit methodological claim with citation.

claim: By comparing spatial patterns formed by Cα-Cβ vectors in differing conformations generated via MD simulation, it is possible to analyze thermal vibrations of residues.
source: By comparing spatial patterns formed by Cα-Cβ vectors in differing conformations generated via MD simulation it is possible to analyze thermal vibrations of residues.
evidence: This is an explicit methodological claim.

claim: Thermal vibrations occur on a sub-nanosecond timescale and are considered to be the foundation of dynamics-driven allosteric effects.
source: These motions occur on a sub-nanosecond timescale and are considered to be the foundation of dynamics-driven allosteric effects, which were predicted by Cooper and Dryden, 1984 and have been observed in multiple proteins (Popovych et al., 2006; Petit et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an explicit claim with citations.

claim: Two major centralities of LSP-based PRNs can contain important information on the local stability (Degree centrality, DC) and global connectivity (Betweenness centrality, BC) of the protein.
source: As we demonstrated, two major centralities of such PRNs can contain important information on the local stability (Degree centrality, DC) and global connectivity (Betweenness centrality, BC) of the protein (Kornev et al., 2022; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an explicit methodological claim with citation and reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Both PRNs showed very similar general structures, featuring dense groups of residues that correlate with the N and C-lobes.
source: Both PRNs showed very similar general structures, featuring dense groups of residues that correlate with the N and C-lobes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the PRN analysis.

claim: The darker color of the αC-β4 loop residues in the F100A mutant indicates the increased level of BC.
source: Notably, the darker color of the αC-β4 loop residues in the F100A mutant indicates the increased level of BC.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the PRN visualization.

claim: Residues from the αF-helix have the highest levels of DC in both the wt C-subunit and F100A.
source: Residues from the αF-helix have the highest levels of DC in both the wt C-subunit and F100A.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the DC analysis.

claim: The αF helix is the most stable structural element of the kinase core and is a major scaffold for the catalytic machinery.
source: This is consistent with the fact that this helix is the most stable structural element of the kinase core and is known to be a major scaffold for the catalytic machinery of these enzymes (Figure 1; Kornev et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact with citation and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The most significant change in the F100A mutant is the increase of BC for the five residues from the αC-β4 loop.
source: The most significant change in the F100A mutant is the increase of BC for the five residues from the αC-β4 loop (highlighted in blue).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the BC analysis.

claim: A set of highly conserved residues show a reduction in their DC, and this reduction is even more pronounced in the BC values in the F100A mutant.
source: Conversely, a set of highly conserved residues (marked in red), previously noted for having the highest levels of BC Kornev et al., 2022, show a reduction in their DC, and this reduction is even more pronounced in the BC values in the F100A mutant.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the centrality analysis.

claim: Positive changes in DC correspond to areas that lose the stability of their Cα-Cβ vectors upon the F100A mutation.
source: Positive changes in DC correspond to areas that lose the stability of their Cα-Cβ vectors upon the mutation (Figure 8A, left, red).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the DC changes with reference to Figure 8A.

claim: Areas that lose stability upon F100A mutation include the catalytic area of the kinase, universally conserved K72, the DFG motif including D184, and the substrate binding site.
source: These include the catalytic area of the kinase, and most importantly, universally conserved K72, the DFG motif, including D184, and the substrate binding site.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the DC analysis.

claim: The ΔDC value for ATP is one of the highest, indicating a significant loss of stability of the adenine ring in the F100A mutant.
source: Notably, the ΔDC value for ATP is one of the highest (Figure 8A, center), indicating a significant loss of stability of the adenine ring in the mutant.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 8A.

claim: Negative changes in ΔDC correspond to areas of PKA that become more stable in the F100A mutant.
source: Negative changes in ΔDC (Figure 8A, right, blue) correspond to areas of PKA that become more stable in the mutant.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with reference to Figure 8A.

claim: Significant negative changes in ΔDC were primarily localized in the αC-β4 loop.
source: Significant changes were primarily localized in the αC-β4 loop.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the DC analysis.

claim: Negative changes in ΔBC values were found in the αC-β4 loop, signifying that the role of the major connecting area between the lobes shifts from the catalytic area to this region.
source: Similarly, negative changes in ΔBC values (Figure 8B, right, blue) were also found in the αC-β4 loop, signifying that the role of the major connecting area between the lobes shifts from the catalytic area (Figure 8B, left, red) to this region.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 8B.

claim: The F100A mutation causes the rigidification of the αC-β4 loop, especially V104 at the tip becomes more stable and rigid.
source: Overall, the F100A mutation causes the rigidification of the αC-β4 loop, especially V104 at the tip becomes more stable and rigid following the mutation of F100.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the LSP analysis.

claim: The major connectors between the N- and C-lobes such as K72 and D184 in the wt protein get impaired and destabilized in response to the F100A mutation.
source: Our analysis suggests that the major connectors between the N- and C-lobes such as K72 from β3 stand (N-lobe) and D184 from the DFG motif (C-lobe) in the wt protein get impaired and destabilized in response to the F100A mutation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the LSP analysis.

claim: The rigidified αC-β4 loop loses the dynamic coupling between the two lobes and the connectivity between both lobes changes.
source: The rigidified αC-β4 loop loses the dynamic coupling between the two lobes and the connectivity between both lobes changes, as seen by V104 and I150, which become the major connector points following the mutation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the LSP analysis.

claim: The F100A mutation changes the allosteric communication between the two lobes.
source: Overall, the mutation at the αC-β4 loop changes the allosteric communication between the two lobes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the LSP analysis.

claim: The LSP results can be interpreted as a disruption of dynamic communication between the two lobes where ATP binding in the N-Lobe comes together with the major catalytic machinery in the C-Lobe.
source: In general, these results can be interpreted as a disruption of dynamic communication between the two lobes where ATP binding in the N-Lobe comes together with the major catalytic machinery in the C-Lobe (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Upon the F100A mutation, a robustly stable region around F102-L106 becomes a dominant connector between the lobes, leading to a significant disruption of correlated dynamics observable in the active site of the wt C-subunit.
source: Upon the mutation, a robustly stable region around F102-L106 becomes a dominant connector between the lobes, leading to a significant disruption of correlated dynamics observable in the active site of the wt C-subunit.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the LSP analysis.

claim: The tip of the αC-β4 loop remained anchored to the αE Helix in all crystal structures including open and closed conformations of the active kinase as well as an inactive unphosphorylated C-subunit.
source: As discussed earlier and as indicated in Figure 4, we did not see significant changes in the αC-β4 loops when we compared our various crystal structures, which included open and closed conformations of the active kinase as well as an inactive unphosphorylated C-subunit. Specifically, the tip of the αC-β4 loops remained anchored to the αE Helix in all of these structures.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to Figure 4.

claim: In the ternary complex with ATP and IP20, the side chain of K105 was toggling (~4.6 A) between two carboxyl groups (E107 and E121).
source: In this structure, the side chain of K105 was toggling (~4.6 A) between two carboxyl groups (E107 and E121), and its backbone carbonyl (the first residue of β4) is hydrogen bonded to the backbone amide of E121 (the last residue of β5) (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to Figure 9B.

claim: In the apo protein, the side chain of K105 has flipped and is now interacting with carbonyls in the β-turn residues and is close to the side chain of N99.
source: While the apo protein showed no major changes in the backbone of the αC-β4 loop, the side chain of K105 has flipped and is now interacting with carbonyls in the β-turn residues. It is also close to the side chain of N99.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation.

claim: Based on the crystal structures, the space near N99 is not sampled by K105 in the wt C-subunit; instead, this space is filled by ordered water molecules.
source: Based on the crystal structures, this space is not sampled by K105 in the wt C-subunit; instead, this space is filled by ordered water molecules.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation.

claim: For the wt C-subunit, there is one global energy minimum based on MD simulations.
source: As seen in Figure 10A, for the wt C-subunit there is one global energy minimum, and the predominant structure for the global energy minimum correlates well with our structure of the ternary complex (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations with reference to Figure 10A.

claim: Based on the simulations, the side chain of K105 interacts predominantly with the side chain of E107 in the wt C-subunit.
source: Based on the simulations, however, instead of toggling between E107 and E121, the side chain of K105 interacts predominantly with the side chain of E107 (Figure 10C), while it rarely samples the side chain of E121 (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations with reference to Figures 10C and 10D.

claim: The F100A mutant shows two energy basins based on MD simulations.
source: In contrast to the wt C-subunit and the apo protein, the mutant shows two energy basins (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations with reference to Figure 10B.

claim: The minor local minimum in the F100A mutant corresponds closely to the wt C-subunit with K105 interacting with E107.
source: The minor local minimum corresponds closely to the wt C-subunit with K105 interacting with E107.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations.

claim: The major global energy minimum in the F100A mutant shows the side chain of K105 interacting with the side chain oxygen of N99 and far from the side chain of E107.
source: In contrast, the major global energy minimum shows the side chain of E105 interacting with the side chain oxygen of N99 and far from the side chain of E107.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from MD simulations.

claim: The F100A mutant has a stronger propensity for K105 to interact with N99.
source: The probability distribution of this interaction with N99 is shown in Figure 10E, which confirms that the mutant has a stronger propensity to interact with N99.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 10E.

claim: The H-bond between Y156 and the backbone amide of N99 is strong in the complex and in the mutant, but destabilized in the apo structure.
source: While the H-bond is strong in the complex and in the mutant, it is surprisingly destabilized in the apo structure.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the probability distribution analysis.

claim: The wt ternary complex behaves similarly to the binary complex, both exhibiting a single global energy minimum.
source: The wt ternary complex, in general, behaves similarly to the binary complex. Both exhibit a single global energy minimum (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 11A.

claim: The F100A mutation shows enhanced dynamics for both binary and ternary complexes.
source: In contrast, the F100A mutation shows enhanced dynamics for both binary and ternary complexes, although there are multiple energy basins in the ternary complex (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 11B.

claim: In the wt binary complex, the side chain of K105 predominately interacts with the side chain of E107.
source: In the wt binary complex, the side chain of K105 predominately interacts with the side chain of E107 (Figure 10C) and interacts more transiently with the side chain of N99 (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with references to Figures 10C and 10E.

claim: In the wt ternary complex, the interactions of K105 and N99 side chains increase while the interaction with E107 decreases.
source: This is in contrast to the wt ternary complex where the interactions of K105 and N99 side chains increase (Figure 11E), while the interaction with E107 decreases (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with references to Figures 11C and 11E.

claim: The side chain of K105 in the wt binary, ternary, and apo states rarely samples the side chain of E121.
source: The side chain of K105 in the wt binary, ternary, and apo states rarely samples the side chain of E121 (Figures 10D and 11D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with references to Figures 10D and 11D.

claim: The hydrogen bond between Y156 and N99 is maintained in the binary and ternary complexes, but broken in the apo protein.
source: The hydrogen bond between Y156 and N99 is also maintained in the binary and ternary complexes, but broken in the apo protein (Figures 10F and 11F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with references to Figures 10F and 11F.

claim: The major difference in the F100A ternary complex is the interaction between K105 and E121, which correlates with the primary energy minimum.
source: The major difference is between K105 and E121, which correlates with the primary energy minimum (Figure 11D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 11D.

claim: The interaction between K105 and E121 is not seen in any of the other complexes.
source: This interaction is not seen in any of the other complexes.
evidence: This is stated as a comparative finding.

claim: In the F100A mutant, the side chain of K105 has a reduced propensity for interacting with the side chain of E107.
source: In addition, the side chain of K105 has a reduced propensity for interacting with the side chain of E107 as shown in the second local minimum.
evidence: This is stated as a finding.

claim: There are no significant changes between Y156 and the backbone amide of N99 in the F100A mutant.
source: Finally, there are no significant changes between Y156 and the backbone amide of N99 in the mutant (Figure 11F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 11F.

claim: The enhanced side chain dynamics of K105 have been observed following the F100A mutation where the side chain of K105 toggles between E121 and N99, and to some extent E107.
source: Hence, the enhanced side chain dynamics of K105 have been observed following the F100A mutation where the side of K105 toggles between E121 and N99, and to some extent E107 (Figure 11G).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with reference to Figure 11G.

claim: The MD simulation results agree with the NMR experimental results and suggest that the F100A mutation alters the dynamic interactions of the αC-β4 loop.
source: In general, these results agree with the NMR experimental results and suggest that the F100A mutation alters the dynamic interactions of the αC-β4 loop, leading to the hypothesis of the disruption in the allosteric communication between both lobes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: The most striking difference based on the MD simulations is the enhanced interaction of K105 with the side chain of E121.
source: The most striking difference, based on the MD simulations, is the enhanced interaction of K105 with the side chain of E121, a key residue that binds directly to the adenine ring of ATP.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the MD simulations.

claim: E121 is a key residue that binds directly to the adenine ring of ATP.
source: The most striking difference, based on the MD simulations, is the enhanced interaction of K105 with the side chain of E121, a key residue that binds directly to the adenine ring of ATP.
evidence: This is stated as a structural fact.

claim: In the crystal structure of the ternary complex, the backbone amide of E121 hydrogen bonds to the backbone carbonyl of K105.
source: As seen in Figure 12A, in the crystal structure of the ternary complex the backbone amide of E121 hydrogen bonds to the backbone carbonyl of K105, while the backbone carbonyl of E121 hydrogen bonds directly to the adenine ring of ATP.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to Figure 12A.

claim: The backbone carbonyl of E121 hydrogen bonds directly to the adenine ring of ATP.
source: As seen in Figure 12A, in the crystal structure of the ternary complex the backbone amide of E121 hydrogen bonds to the backbone carbonyl of K105, while the backbone carbonyl of E121 hydrogen bonds directly to the adenine ring of ATP.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to Figure 12A.

claim: The αC-β4 loop should be carefully examined in all protein kinases as it is a focal point for linking ATP binding to peptide/protein binding and for opening and closing of the catalytic cleft.
source: Overall, our work suggests that the αC-β4 loop should be carefully examined in all protein kinases as it is a focal point for linking ATP binding to peptide/protein binding and for opening and closing of the catalytic cleft.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the work.

claim: The enhanced flexibility of the side chain of K105 may be an initial step that leads to subsequent changes in the backbone dynamics.
source: We thus predict that the enhanced flexibility of the side chain of K105 may be an initial step that leads to subsequent changes in the backbone dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction.

claim: The potential importance of both N99 and K105 in mediating changes in dynamics needs to be experimentally validated biochemically, by NMR, and by further computational analyses.
source: The potential importance of both N99 and K105 in mediating changes in dynamics also needs to be experimentally validated biochemically, by NMR, and by further computational analyses.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction.

claim: The hydrogen bond between the side chain of Y156 and the backbone amide of N99 is very stable in the binary and ternary complexes and in the mutant but weakened in the apo protein.
source: The graphs of the hydrogen bond between the side chain of Y156 and the backbone amide of N99 show that this bond is very stable in the binary and ternary complexes and in the mutant but weakened in the apo protein (Figure 10E), and this would also be consistent with the prediction that the β-turn may be more flexible in the absence of ligands but stabilized in a different way in the F100A mutant.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to Figure 10E.

claim: The β-turn may be more flexible in the absence of ligands but stabilized in a different way in the F100A mutant.
source: The graphs of the hydrogen bond between the side chain of Y156 and the backbone amide of N99 show that this bond is very stable in the binary and ternary complexes and in the mutant but weakened in the apo protein (Figure 10E), and this would also be consistent with the prediction that the β-turn may be more flexible in the absence of ligands but stabilized in a different way in the F100A mutant.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction.

claim: The αC-β4 loop is a good potential therapeutic target as the specific residues such as N99 and K105 that are mechanistically important are different in all kinases.
source: The αC-β4 loop is also a good potential therapeutic target as the specific residues such as N99 and K105 that are mechanistically important are different in all kinases in contrast to the conserved residues such as K72 and D184 that position the phosphates of ATP.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: The importance of αC-β4 loop is reinforced because cancer mutations are located here.
source: The importance of αC-β4 loop is also reinforced because the cancer mutations are located here (Ruan and Kannan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence with citation.

claim: LSP could be used as a predictor of dynamics for any mutant or for carrying out an alanine scan of any protein.
source: Finally, given the extremely close correlation of the LSP analysis with the NMR results and the Markov State model predictions, as well as our principal component analysis (PCA) of the wt and F100A mutant, we suggest that LSP could be used as a predictor of dynamics for any mutant or even for carrying out an alanine scan of any protein.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion for future applications.

claim: LSP is rapid and relatively inexpensive and could easily be used as an initial screen to identify potentially important residues that contribute to dynamics.
source: In contrast, LSP is rapid and relatively inexpensive and could easily be used as an initial screen to identify potentially important residues that contribute to dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the LSP method.
